I'm an Australia and we more or less did away with cheques years ago. You can still get them, and some people in the bush use them, but the majority of businesses won't accept them because it's too hard to chase up the money if they bounce. I don't know of anyone who really misses them, but that is because our infrastructure is fairly good. Most companies (even small businesses) take credit/debit card (EFTPOS), including allowing you to pay online or over the phone. Most large companies also allow you to pay bills in person at the post office. For the rare scenarios where a cheque is required (e.g. paying rental bond), personal cheques generally aren't accepted anyway (there's no guarantee you have the money in your account), so you just pay the $5 for a bank cheque. For other scenarios (like buying a second hand car), you can either transfer the money directly to the person's bank account and show them the receipt, bring cash if you feel comfortable, or again pay for a bank cheque.

I know it would never catch on, it's really more of a wild dream than realistic hope. But after learning Spanish where everything is pronounced consistently with how it's spelled, and learning of other languages that do the same, it doesn't make sense to me that any language should be less consistent. After all, isn't text supposed to be a symbolic representation of the spoken language? Doesn't it make sense that it should very closely mirror the spoken words from which it is derived? The poem "The Chaos" by Gerard Nolst Trenité demonstrates my issues with English exactly.
What about Chinese, in which the writing system isn't supposed to represent the sound? That writing system is no more difficult than English.

That's an apples and oranges comparison in my opinion. Written Chinese evolved as a standard way for people to communicate across vastly differing regional dialects. By having the written language represent the ideas in a pictorial sense, it was an apt tool for that job. Written English is a representation of a much more (though not entirely) unified spoken language, and as such would likely benefit from the clarity provided by a system by which the written more closely approximates the spoken.
Hopefully this doesn't come across as argumentative, I'm just sharing my opinions.

Right, but nowadays Chinese writing isn't used for vastly different dialects; mandarin has its own (two) writing systems and Cantonese has its own system, albeit largely based on traditional Chinese. But people read and write these languages every day without issues, and they are no harder to learn than something like Spanish or Finnish.

All I'm saying is that I fail to see how a phonetic writing system can be better. In my opinion, no writing system is better or worse. It is impossible to describe any aspect of language with those terms.
I'm not trying to say a phonetic system is better than something like Chinese, I'm trying to say a good phonetic system is better than the half-assed sort of phonetic garbage that is English.

But English writing was never meant to be one-to-one phonetic, unless you're talking about our runic writing system.

And there's something to be said for preserving the original spelling and pronunciation of loanwords as well as English does. Don't you think?
